data indicate that the CCM coating introduces an additional diffusion barrier, consistent with a release
mechanism driven by hydrophobic partitioning and structural stabilization rather than chemical bond
cleavage. Third, to visualize intracellular trafficking and dissociation of PROTAC from
endosomal/lysosomal compartments into the cytosol, we employed FITC-labeled BRD4-PROTAC
together with immunofluorescence labeling of Rab5 (early endosomes) and LAMP1 (lysosomes),
followed by time-resolved confocal imaging and Pearson’s correlation analysis. At early time points,
BRD4-PROTAC fluorescence strongly colocalized with Rab5-positive vesicles, indicating uptake
through classical endocytic pathways into early endosomes. With prolonged incubation, the
fluorescence pattern gradually transitioned from punctate vesicular localization to a more diffuse
cytosolic distribution, accompanied by reduced colocalization with LAMP1 (Figure S14B–E). These
observations indicate partial lysosomal escape and progressive cytosolic accumulation of PROTAC,
consistent with a microenvironment-triggered dissociation mechanism, whereby mild acidic conditions
weaken hydrophobic core stability and facilitate drug release. Finally, to directly link release and
intracellular transport to functional BRD4 degradation, we added time-course Western blot analyses
comparing free dBET1, PM, and CCM@PM treatments. Free dBET1 induced a marked reduction in
BRD4 protein levels starting at 6 h, with near-complete depletion by 24–48 h. In contrast, PM- and
CCM@PM-treated cells exhibited time-dependent BRD4 downregulation with slower and more
gradual degradation kinetics (Figure S14F–G). Importantly, the temporal profiles of BRD4 degradation
closely matched the corresponding release kinetics of each carrier, demonstrating that PROTAC
released from the nanocarrier remains functionally active and that release dynamics are temporally
coupled to downstream protein degradation. Collectively, through the addition of FTIR
characterization, BET–DFT pore structure analysis, elution assays (Figure S10B, 11, and 12), as well
as release kinetics, intracellular distribution, and BRD4 degradation time-course analyses (Figure
S14A–G), we systematically elucidate the noncovalent, microenvironment-responsive release
mechanism of PROTAC from CCM@PM and Rh-Gel@CCM@PM. These integrated data establish a
clear temporal and mechanistic link between structural features, release behavior, intracellular
availability, and functional BRD4 degradation, thereby fully addressing the reviewer’s concern.
9. Source and applicability of neonatal chondrocyte membranes
CCM is derived from P1 primary chondrocyte. Please address potential differences between neonatal
14
and adult or diseased cartilage with respect to receptor and adhesion profiles. Provide evidence that
supports applicability in diseased adult cartilage, or comparative data using adult or OA-derived
membranes.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this constructive comment. In the revised manuscript, we have
added a detailed rationale in the Methods section (“Preparation of cartilage cell membrane (CCM)”)
to clarify the selection of P1 primary chondrocytes as the membrane source. Specifically, P1 primary
chondrocytes were chosen to ensure membrane integrity and batch-to-batch consistency, thereby
providing a stable adhesion and receptor phenotype that minimizes preparation-related variability. We
further clarify that the isolated CCM retains key membrane proteins and adhesion-related molecules
after preparation, including receptors, integrins, and glycosaminoglycan-binding components, which
are essential for constructing the subsequent membrane-camouflaged delivery system. Regarding
applicability, based on the results of the present study, Rh-Gel@CCM@PM fabricated using
membranes derived from P1 primary murine chondrocytes exhibited good biocompatibility in adult
mice (Supplementary Figure 17) and effectively alleviated cartilage degeneration and pain-related
behaviors in both DMM- and MIA-induced osteoarthritis models (Figures S7 and S8). These findings
support the feasibility of using P1 primary chondrocyte-derived membranes for applications in adult
mice. Nevertheless, we have also added a discussion of potential limitations in the Discussion section:
“With regard to membrane source-dependent variability, neonatal and adult or osteoarthritic cartilage
may differ in receptor density, integrin/adhesion profiles, and glycosylation patterns, which could
influence interactions between membrane-camouflaged nanoparticles and cartilage matrix or cells.
In this study, P1-derived CCM was employed to ensure membrane structural integrity and preparation
consistency. Notably, the observed intra-articular retention and therapeutic efficacy in disease models,
together with molecular and phenotypic validation in human primary chondrocytes, support the
translational relevance of this strategy in adult and OA contexts. Future work will systematically
compare membrane characteristics derived from adult or OA cartilage sources and evaluate their
impact on cellular uptake, tissue retention, and therapeutic outcomes, thereby strengthening the
translational foundation of this delivery platform”.
10. In vivo distribution and clearance
Only local joint retention imaging is presented at several time points. Whole-body biodistribution,
organ tropism, clearance routes, and systemic safety have not been established.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. The primary objective of this study
15
was to evaluate the intra-articular retention behavior of Rh-Gel@CCM@PM within the joint
microenvironment and its therapeutic effects targeting the BRD4/Nav1.7 axis. Accordingly, our in vivo
experiments initially focused on local retention and therapeutic efficacy within the joint cavity. As the
joint space represents a relatively enclosed compartment with limited fluid exchange, its drug delivery
behavior differs substantially from that of systemic circulation, and local retention directly reflects
effective intra-articular exposure of the delivery system. In response to the reviewer’s comment, we
have revised Figure S17C by replacing the localized joint images with whole-body in vivo fluorescence
images. These data clearly show no appreciable signal accumulation in other major organs. In addition,
we performed ex vivo fluorescence imaging of harvested tissues to further assess biodistribution. The
results demonstrate that none of the nanoparticle formulations exhibited detectable fluorescence
enrichment in other organs (Figure S17E). Notably, among all tested formulations, Rh-
Gel@CCM@PM exhibited the longest intra-articular retention time, the highest fluorescence intensity,
and the slowest signal decay rate. Quantitative fitting analysis further revealed a significantly
prolonged intra-articular half-life for Rh-Gel@CCM@PM (Figure S17D). Furthermore, in
Supplementary Figure 18, we evaluated the in vivo biocompatibility of Rh-Gel@CCM@PM, showing
no evident adverse effects on major organs, thereby supporting its favorable biosafety profile.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
This study is the first to reveal the pathological mechanism of osteoarthritis (OA) in which BRD4
regulates Nav1.7 expression through histone acetylation. It proposes a novel regulatory axis of "BRD4-
histone acetylation-Nav1.7-metabolic imbalance," broadening the research perspective on epigenetic
regulation in OA. While the study demonstrates certain innovativeness, the following critical
shortcomings and issues need to be carefully addressed before considering acceptance:
As an epigenetic regulator, BRD4 may participate in the progression of OA by regulating multiple
downstream target genes. In addition to Nav1.7, are there other key target genes (such as inflammation-
related genes IL-6 and MMP13) that collaboratively mediate the pro-OA effects of BRD4? GSEA
analysis of whole transcriptome data after BRD4 knockout should be supplemented to clarify the
weight of Nav1.7 in the downstream pathways of BRD4.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. We fully agree that, as an epigenetic
regulator, BRD4 is likely to exert its pro-osteoarthritis (OA) effects through multiple downstream
targets. As described in the manuscript, our multidimensional experimental data indicate that BRD4 not
16
only regulates Nav1.7 transcription but also positively modulates the expression of inflammatory
mediators (such as IL-6 and IL-1β) and matrix-degrading enzymes, including MMP13. In the TNF-α–
induced chondrocyte model, BRD4 knockdown significantly reduced the expression of IL-6 and IL-1β
while concomitantly upregulating cartilage anabolic markers SOX9 and type II collagen (COL II).
In contrast, pharmacological activation of Nav1.7 partially reversed the anti-inflammatory and pro-
anabolic effects induced by BRD4 silencing, suggesting that BRD4 contributes to OA progression
through coordinated regulation of the Nav1.7 pathway and inflammatory signaling networks.
Consistently, immunohistochemical analyses in vivo further demonstrated that either BRD4
knockdown or PROTAC-mediated BRD4 degradation led to decreased expression of MMP13 and IL-
6, providing additional support for this conclusion. In response to the reviewer’s recommendation, we
have also added a genome-wide transcriptomic analysis following BRD4 knockout, including gene set
enrichment analysis (GSEA) (new Figure S4I in the revised manuscript). The results show that BRD4
depletion is associated with coordinated suppression of pathways related to ion transmembrane
transport, cellular energy metabolism, and extracellular matrix remodeling. These transcriptomic
changes are in good agreement with our in vitro and in vivo observations, including reduced Nav1.7
expression and decreased IL-6 and MMP13 levels. Collectively, these findings further support the
notion that BRD4 acts as an upstream regulatory hub in OA pathogenesis, exerting multi-layered
control over metabolic, inflammatory, and matrix-remodeling processes.
Nav1.7 is traditionally known as a pain-related channel in neurons, and its functional validation in
chondrocytes requires more rigorous investigation. For example, are the electrophysiological
characteristics of Nav1.7 in chondrocytes consistent with those in neurons? Beyond mitochondrial
function and metabolic imbalance, does Nav1.7 participate in OA by regulating chondrocyte
mechanosensation or calcium signaling?
Response: We thank the reviewer for this professional and thoughtful suggestion. The primary
objective of the present study was to elucidate the epigenetic regulatory cascade linking BRD4,
histone acetylation, and Scn9a (Nav1.7) transcription, and to evaluate its impact on chondrocyte metabolic
homeostasis and tissue-level phenotypes. Accordingly, our experimental design prioritized molecular
and functional readouts, including BRD4/Nav1.7 expression, cartilage anabolic and catabolic markers
(COL II and MMP13), mitochondrial and metabolic indices, and in vivo therapeutic outcomes.
Electrophysiological characterization (e.g., membrane currents or action potentials), as well as
mechanobiological or calcium signaling-focused assays, were therefore beyond the intended scope of
17
the current work. Notably, our existing data demonstrate that TNF-α–induced sodium currents in
ATDC5 chondrocytes are predominantly mediated by Nav1.7 (Figures 2F–K), which is consistent with
previously published reports (PMID: 39559752; PMID: 32128393; PMID: 38172636). Regarding the
possibility that Nav1.7 contributes to osteoarthritis (OA) progression through mechanosensation or
calcium signaling, recent work by Chuan-ju Liu et al. (PMID: 38172636) has shown that Nav1.7
blockade modulates intracellular Ca²⁺ signaling and the chondrocyte secretome, thereby influencing
chondrocyte biology and OA progression. These findings support the notion that Nav1.7 may
participate in OA pathogenesis via mechanical or calcium-dependent pathways. While direct
investigation of these signaling modalities was not included in the present study, we agree that they
represent important and compelling directions for future research. Building upon the current findings,
we plan to further explore the mechanistic links between Nav1.7 activity, calcium signaling,
mechanotransduction, and cartilage degeneration in subsequent studies.
The targeting specificity of the materials used by the authors is insufficient. For chronic diseases,
targeting specificity is a critical issue due to the need for long-term use. Therefore, the authors should
conduct in-depth research on targeting specificity and long-term toxic side effects.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important and thoughtful suggestion. The primary objective
of this study was to validate the pathogenic cascade linking BRD4, histone acetylation, and Scn9a
(Nav1.7) transcription, and to evaluate the feasibility of local intra-articular intervention targeting this
axis. Accordingly, at the materials design level, we prioritized a strategy combining intra-articular local
administration, in situ gelation–mediated retention, and cartilage cell membrane (CCM) camouflage to
achieve functional “on-site enrichment” within the joint cavity. Using multimodal evidence, we
demonstrated effective local exposure and favorable tolerability of the delivery system. Specifically,
Supplementary Figure 17 shows that CCM@PM exhibits strong adhesion to cartilage tissue, enhanced
penetration, and prolonged intra-articular retention, with minimal off-target accumulation, supporting
its cartilage-specific distribution. In Supplementary Figure 18, we further demonstrate that Rh-
Gel@CCM@PM does not induce detectable adverse effects in major organs following repeated intra-
articular administration. In addition, we included long-term in vitro cytotoxicity assessments, which
showed that treatment with 1 μM dBET1 did not elicit long-term cytotoxic effects in ATDC5
chondrocytes or murine synovial mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) (Supplementary Figure 8G–H).
Collectively, these results provide initial evidence that Rh-Gel@CCM@PM possesses favorable tissue
targeting and a low risk of systemic toxicity. At the same time, we fully acknowledge that the present
18
findings do not immediately support clinical translation. We agree that, particularly in the context of
chronic diseases, long-term targeting specificity and cumulative toxicity are critical considerations.
Due to the scope of the current study, we did not perform detailed quantitative analyses of receptor- or
adhesion-mediated specificity, nor comprehensive systemic pharmacokinetic and toxicological
evaluations. We have supplemented the future direction in our revised Discussion section:
“Nevertheless, several limitations remain. Long-term toxicity and immunogenicity have not yet been
systematically evaluated. Future studies will focus on quantifying targeting specificity through
receptor-blocking or competitive binding assays, as well as comparisons between homologous and
heterologous membrane sources. Comprehensive evaluations of systemic biodistribution,
pharmacokinetics, and organ toxicity, including long-term and repeated dosing studies, will also be
required. In addition, comparative validation using adult- or OA-derived membrane sources will be
performed to further strengthen evidence for targeting precision and long-term safety”.
There are many small molecule inhibitors of BRD4. Why must a BRD4 degrader be used? Have small
molecule inhibitors been compared for the treatment of OA?
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important suggestion. The choice of a BRD4 degrader rather
than a small-molecule inhibitor in this study was driven by both mechanistic considerations and the
intended application context. Currently, the clinical development of pan-BRD4 inhibitors has been
limited by adverse effects, with several BET inhibitors (e.g., MK-8628) reported to induce dose-
limiting toxicities such as thrombocytopenia, diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting (PMID: 39918129; PMID:
26367796). In contrast, BD1- or BD2-selective BRD4 inhibitors have been developed to reduce
toxicity by more precise modulation of bromodomain activity, thereby minimizing off-target effects
and pathway bypass activation, and have shown improved safety profiles compared with pan-BRD4
inhibitors (doi:10.1016/j.rechem.2025.102670). However, BRD4 contains not only two bromodomains
(BD1 and BD2), which mediate recognition of acetylated lysine residues and chromatin association,
but also a histone acetyltransferase (HAT) domain capable of catalyzing histone lysine acetylation
(PMID: 30466442). In addition, BRD4 plays non–bromodomain-dependent scaffold roles in
transcriptional complex assembly and phase separation. Therefore, selectively blocking bromodomain
interactions alone may be insufficient to fully abrogate BRD4 function. In contrast, BRD4 degraders
eliminate the BRD4 protein itself via the ubiquitin–proteasome pathway, enabling more comprehensive
suppression of the upstream regulatory cascade linking BRD4, histone acetylation, and Scn9a (Nav1.7)
transcription, while reducing the risk of functional rebound due to residual BRD4 activity. In the
19
context of osteoarthritis, a chronic and localized disease, our strategy combines intra-articular injection
with an in situ gelation system to achieve sustained local exposure. Under these conditions, an event-
driven degradation strategy is particularly advantageous compared with occupancy-driven inhibition, as
it allows prolonged pathway suppression at lower dosing frequency. Although we did not directly
compare BRD4 degraders with small-molecule BRD4 inhibitors in the present study, we agree that
such comparisons would be valuable for further optimization of therapeutic strategies. Accordingly, we
plan to conduct comparative efficacy and safety evaluations between dBET1 and representative BRD4
inhibitors under equivalent local exposure conditions in future work to further support translational
development.
20
